# Arne Furumark

Arne Furumark (1903–1982) was a prominent Swedish classical archaeologist who specialized in the prehistory of the Aegean region , . He spent his entire academic career at Uppsala University, where he became Professor of Classical Archaeology and Ancient History in 1952, a position he held until his retirement in 1970 , , . His most enduring contribution to the field is his meticulously detailed typology of Mycenaean pottery, first published in 1941, which established a foundational chronological framework for Late Bronze Age Greece and remains a reference point in Aegean ceramic studies more than eight decades later , , . Beyond this seminal work, Furumark was an active excavator, notably leading campaigns at Sinda in Cyprus, and demonstrated intellectual agility by becoming one of the earliest influential scholars to embrace and integrate the revolutionary findings of the decipherment of Linear B , . His long tenure at Uppsala and leadership role at the Swedish Institute at Athens during the post-war era positioned him at the center of international Aegean scholarship, making him a key figure in the development of the discipline during the mid-20th century , .

## Biography and Academic Career

Arne Furumark's life and career are defined by a deep and sustained commitment to classical archaeology, primarily centered at Uppsala University in Sweden , . Born Josef Arne Gerdt Furumark on September 26, 1903, in Kristiania (now Oslo), which was then part of the Norway-Sweden union, his early life coincided with a period of significant cultural and political change in Scandinavia , . He entered Uppsala University in 1925, marking the beginning of a lifelong academic association with the institution that would become his professional home . His education culminated in the award of a doctorate in 1939, based on his dissertation titled *Studies in Aegean Decorative Art: Antecedent and Sources of the Mycenaean Ceramic Decoration* , . This early work foreshadowed the monumental typological project for which he would later become world-renowned, demonstrating from the outset a profound focus on the artistic and stylistic evolution of Aegean material culture.

Following the completion of his doctorate, Furumark's academic career advanced steadily within the Department of Classical Archaeology at Uppsala University. In the same year he earned his PhD, 1939, he was appointed Associate Professor, a position that allowed him to begin shaping the next generation of archaeologists while further developing his own research program . His expertise and reputation grew rapidly, leading to his appointment as Professor of Classical Archaeology and Ancient History in 1952 , , . This promotion marked his elevation to the highest rank in his department, a status he maintained for twenty years until his retirement in 1970 , . His long and stable career at Uppsala provided him with the institutional stability necessary to produce his definitive works and to mentor students, solidifying his position as a central figure in Scandinavian Aegean studies .

Beyond his primary role at Uppsala, Furumark held significant leadership positions that underscored his standing within the international archaeological community. Most notably, he served as Director of the Swedish Institute at Athens from 1956 to 1957 , . This period was particularly significant, as it placed him in direct contact with the epicenter of Aegean archaeology just as the field was being transformed by the decipherment of Linear B . His directorship demonstrates that he was not only a respected scholar but also an administrator capable of leading a key Nordic institution dedicated to the study of ancient Greece. During his time in Athens, he was actively engaged in the scholarly discourse surrounding the new linguistic discoveries, corresponding with figures like Michael Ventris and John Chadwick, and attending the very first international colloquium dedicated to Mycenaean texts in 1956 , . His career trajectory reflects a consistent pattern of growth, from student to influential professor and director, cementing his legacy as a pillar of 20th-century classical archaeology.

Furumark's life concluded in Uppsala, Sweden, on October 8, 1982 . His passing marked the end of an era for the discipline he had helped shape. Throughout his career, he remained a prolific author and editor, contributing numerous articles and overseeing the publication of excavation reports from institutions like the Swedish Institute in Rome . His work continues to be recognized for its methodological rigor and its foundational importance to the study of Aegean prehistory. His long association with Uppsala University is well-documented, with his name appearing alongside other distinguished scholars affiliated with the department, such as Torgny Säve-Söderbergh and Axel W. Persson . This institutional context is crucial for understanding the environment in which his most important ideas were developed and disseminated over several decades.

## The Furumark Classification System and Its Impact

The cornerstone of Arne Furumark's scholarly legacy is his classification system for Mycenaean pottery, introduced in two pivotal 1941 publications: *The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification* and *The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery* , , . This work represented a monumental achievement in Aegean archaeology, providing a systematic and exhaustive framework for the typological analysis of Late Helladic ceramics , . The system's comprehensiveness was unprecedented; it meticulously cataloged 103 distinct vessel forms, 336 variations in shape, various syntactical arrangements of decorative elements, and 78 unique motifs . These elements were organized into eight chronologically distinct stylistic phases, creating a finely tuned relative chronology that could be applied across the entire Aegean basin . By establishing these stylistic sequences, Furumark provided archaeologists with a powerful tool to date pottery assemblages from settlements and graves with a high degree of precision .

The impact of this system was immediate and profound. It directly enabled the establishment of a robust absolute chronology for the Mycenaean civilization. Because Mycenaean pottery was widely exported, sherds of Furumark's typified styles were found in well-dated contexts in Egypt and the Levant, such as at Tell el-Amarna, Gurob, and Saqqara , . By correlating the stylistic sequences identified by Furumark with these secure Egyptian dates, scholars could anchor the entire Mycenaean timeline, transforming it from a series of relative associations into a coherent historical narrative . The system's significance was recognized swiftly within the academic community. Within three years of its publication, a detailed book review appeared in the *American Journal of Archaeology*, confirming its immediate acceptance and engagement by transatlantic Aegean archaeologists . Elizabeth Wace French, a leading student of Mycenaean pottery, adapted Furumark's taxonomy to analyze highly fragmentary settlement deposits at Mycenae, using his framework to make groundbreaking subdivisions of LH IIIB and refine the dating of LH IIIC . Her students, including Penelope Mountjoy, further built upon this foundation, demonstrating the system's lasting influence on generations of ceramic specialists .

Despite its age, the Furumark classification system retains a remarkable degree of operational relevance today, even as it has been subject to critical reassessment. It is explicitly cited and used in contemporary scholarly publications, including a 2021 archaeometric study that employed "Furumark numbers" (FM and FS) to visually identify Late Helladic sherds from the site of Asine . Furthermore, it serves as the baseline chronological framework against which later transitional phases, such as the contested Submycenaean style, are debated and evaluated . However, modern scholarship has also highlighted significant limitations. The system is now generally regarded as "mostly superseded," criticized for oversimplifying the vast variations within many of its broad categories, which can lead to confusion in application . Some scholars have questioned its utility for determining vessel function, noting that its formal typology was not designed for such analyses . Others have pointed out that it did not address raw materials or forming techniques, representing a gap in its holistic approach to ceramic studies . A critique of a 2011 book on Mycenaean settlement argued that Furumark’s typology is not designed to address vessel function, chronology, or form development . This dual assessment—of enduring foundational value combined with acknowledged shortcomings—defines the complex legacy of his typological work. It stands as a testament to the power of rigorous classification in an earlier phase of archaeology while also serving as a benchmark against which the more nuanced methodologies of the present day are measured.

## Methodological Approach and Intellectual Context

To fully appreciate the nature and significance of Arne Furumark's work, it is essential to situate it within the dominant intellectual currents of 20th-century European archaeology. His career and methodology were profoundly shaped by the prevailing school of thought known as culture-historical archaeology, which dominated the discipline from the late 19th century until it was largely superseded by processualism in the mid-20th century . This paradigm emphasized the classification of material culture—particularly pottery—into discrete, definable "archaeological cultures." These cultures were often interpreted as representing distinct ethnic groups, with changes between them explained primarily through migration or cultural diffusion rather than internal development . Furumark's entire project of creating a detailed typology for Mycenaean pottery is a quintessential example of this approach. His goal was to define 'archaeological cultures' via regularly associated traits, using inductive reasoning and typological classification to trace the evolution of Minoan, Helladic, and Cycladic cultures as distinct entities . His classification system was thus not merely a descriptive tool but a theoretical instrument for ordering the archaeological record into culturally coherent units and tracing their temporal succession.

A deeper analysis of Furumark's epistemology reveals a more sophisticated interplay of ideas. His work exhibits clear hallmarks of logical positivism, an early appropriation of analytical philosophy into the practice of archaeology . This manifests in his drive for a systematic, objective, and empirically grounded classification system. The sheer scale and detail of his 1941 publication—the enumeration of hundreds of forms, shapes, and motifs—reflects a positivist desire to impose order and create a reliable, verifiable framework for interpreting the past . His approach has been characterized as a form of "negotiated positivism," a synthesis between the rigorous classification of logical positivism and the overarching cultural frameworks of culture-historical archaeology . This distinguishes his work from the later, more overtly anti-positivist tenets of processual archaeology, which sought to explain cultural phenomena through scientific models of human behavior rather than simply describing their material expressions . Furumark did not adopt processualism wholeheartedly; instead, his work represents a bridge between these two paradigms, retaining the core logic of culture-historical theory while infusing it with a greater degree of analytical precision derived from positivist principles.

This methodological context is crucial for understanding both the strengths and weaknesses of Furumark's contributions. His strength lay in his ability to create a monumental and durable framework that brought unprecedented chronological clarity to the study of Mycenaean pottery . By meticulously documenting stylistic changes, he provided archaeologists with a powerful tool for sequencing material from diverse sites. However, the limitations of his approach are also rooted in its intellectual origins. The culture-historical focus on classifying artifacts into discrete cultural packages sometimes led to an oversimplification of complex social processes. For instance, his typology, while excellent for formal shape analysis, did not initially address questions of production technology, raw material sourcing, or vessel function, areas that have become central to modern ceramic studies , . The critiques that label his system as potentially confusing due to its broad categories may stem from an attempt to apply his rigid typological framework to contexts where cultural boundaries were more fluid than his model suggested . Therefore, Furumark's legacy is inseparable from the intellectual climate of his time. He was a master of the tools available to him, producing a work of immense utility that nonetheless reflects the theoretical assumptions and limitations of the culture-historical era from which it emerged.

## Fieldwork and Regional Studies

While Arne Furumark is best known for his typological work, his contributions to Aegean prehistory extend significantly beyond the analysis of pottery. He was an active and engaged field archaeologist whose excavations and regional studies provided crucial data for understanding the broader historical landscape of the Bronze Age Aegean and its periphery. His most substantial and influential fieldwork was conducted as part of the Swedish Cyprus Expedition, where he played a key role in defining the character of the Late Bronze Age on the island , . Between 1947 and 1948, and again from 1962 to 1963, Furumark directed excavations at the site of Sinda, located in western Cyprus , . His work at Sinda was instrumental in reinforcing the "Mycenaean colonisation" paradigm for post-palatial Cyprus . In his 1944 article, "The Mycenaean IIIC Pottery and its Relation to Cypriote Fabrics," he provided a foundational analysis that directly linked Mycenaean ceramic typology to the local Cypriot fabric, thereby establishing a clear and quantifiable link between the Aegean mainland and the island's material culture during this period , , . This work was so central to the expedition's interpretation that it was cited alongside publications by other leading members of the team, such as Erik Gjerstad and Paul Åström . Further insights from his Cypriot campaigns were presented in his 1965 paper, "The Excavations at Sinda. Some Historical Results," which connected the ceramic evidence from Sinda to broader interpretations of population movements and socio-political change in post-palatial Cyprus , .

In addition to his extensive work in Cyprus, Furumark participated in excavations elsewhere in the eastern Mediterranean. In 1948, he conducted a short but significant excavation at Hala Sultan Tekke, another important Late Bronze Age site in Cyprus [)]. During this brief campaign, he discovered a large pithos, adding to the corpus of knowledge about the site's occupation and material culture [)]. This activity demonstrates his continued involvement in Cypriot archaeology throughout the 1940s. Beyond the Aegean, Furumark also pursued research in other regions, showcasing the breadth of his interests. In 1947, he published *Det äldsta Italien* (The Earliest Italy), a pioneering post-World War II study of Italian prehistory , . This work extended his methodological expertise beyond the Aegean and contributed to the wider study of the Mediterranean world. His scholarly output also included detailed studies of Aegean history itself. His 1950 paper, "The Settlement at Ialysos and Aegean History c. 1550–1400 B.C.," was a landmark study that anchored the Late Helladic and Late Minoan ceramic sequences to a specific period , . By doing so, he provided a crucial synchronistic framework that has been invaluable for debates concerning the absolute dating of events like the eruption of Thera, helping to align Aegean chronology with the well-established timelines of the Egyptian Second Intermediate Period and New Kingdom . Through these varied field projects and regional studies, Furumark demonstrated himself to be a versatile scholar who applied his meticulous methods to a wide range of archaeological contexts, enriching our understanding of the Bronze Age Mediterranean far beyond the confines of his famous pottery typology.

## Role in the Study of Aegean Scripts

One of the most fascinating aspects of Arne Furumark's career is his active and enthusiastic engagement with the monumental decipherment of Linear B, the script used to write an early form of Greek at sites like Knossos and Pylos. Far from being a passive observer of this revolution in Aegean studies, Furumark was an integral part of the scholarly network that embraced and disseminated the new knowledge. His recognition as an expert in Mycenaean archaeology is evidenced by his inclusion on the targeted distribution list for Michael Ventris's seminal 'Work Note 15' in 1951 . This document, which outlined the phonetic grid methodology and morphological analysis that would lead to the decipherment, was sent to a select group of 31 leading scholars, including prominent figures like Carl Blegen, Alice Kober, and John Chadwick , . Being among this elite cohort immediately after the decipherment was announced publicly by Ventris in a BBC interview on July 1, 1952, signifies that Furumark was considered a key authority whose opinion would carry significant weight within the academic community .

Following the public announcement of the decipherment, Furumark quickly moved to incorporate its findings into his own archaeological interpretations. His correspondence with both Michael Ventris and John Chadwick, the latter of whom would famously co-author the definitive grammar of Mycenaean Greek, is preserved in archival collections at the Program in Aegean Scripts and Prehistory (PASP) at the University of Cincinnati and the Uppsala University Archives , , . This exchange of letters documents his early endorsement of the Greek interpretation of Linear B, positioning him as an influential validator of the decipherment within the archaeological world . His rapid integration of the new linguistic evidence demonstrates intellectual agility and a clear understanding of how the decipherment would fundamentally reshape the field, overturning Sir Arthur Evans's long-held belief that the language was non-Greek . Furumark's support for the new interpretation helped legitimize it among his peers.

Furthermore, Furumark's participation in the nascent scholarly community formed around the decipherment was direct and significant. He attended the first-ever international colloquium on Mycenaean texts, held at Gif-sur-Yvette in France in April 1956 . This conference was a historic gathering, bringing together the pioneers of the field for the first time, and it was the only such event attended by Michael Ventris before his untimely death in September of that year . Furumark’s presence at this exclusive meeting places him within a small, foundational cohort of scholars, alongside institutional leaders and philologists from across Europe, including Émile Benveniste and Georges Dumézil . This engagement underscores that his interest in Aegean scripts was not limited to his primary work on pottery. He was also deeply involved in the study of the undeciphered Linear A script, publishing a two-volume work on the subject in 1956, *Linear A und die altkretische Sprache* . His multifaceted engagement with Aegean writing systems—from applying the new Greek decipherment to his own work to studying the older Minoan script—paints a picture of a truly comprehensive scholar who was at the forefront of the most exciting intellectual developments in classical archaeology during his lifetime.

## Major Publications and Scholarly Legacy

Arne Furumark's scholarly output was extensive and covered a wide range of topics within Aegean prehistory. His publications reflect his dual expertise in ceramic typology and broader historical archaeology, as well as his engagement with the study of Aegean scripts. The table below summarizes some of his most significant works, highlighting the scope and depth of his contributions to the field.

Furumark's legacy is that of a foundational figure whose work provided the essential chronological scaffolding for Aegean archaeology for much of the 20th century. His 1941 pottery classification remains a touchstone for scholars, a testament to the power of meticulous typological analysis in an earlier phase of the discipline , . While modern methodologies have moved beyond the strictures of culture-historical archaeology, his system's enduring relevance highlights the quality and comprehensiveness of his work . At the same time, the critiques leveled against it serve as a valuable lesson in the evolution of archaeological thought, illustrating the shift towards more holistic approaches that consider vessel function, technology, and social context , . Beyond his typology, Furumark's legacy is also one of intellectual adaptability and wide-ranging scholarship. He successfully transitioned from a career focused on material culture to embracing the linguistic revolution of the Linear B decipherment, integrating its findings into his archaeological interpretations with remarkable speed and insight . His work in Cyprus, Italy, and on Minoan religion demonstrates a versatility that prevented him from becoming a narrow specialist , , . In summary, Arne Furumark was a master of his craft, a leader in his field, and a pivotal figure whose influence continues to be felt in the ongoing study of the ancient Aegean.

By meticulously documenting stylistic changes, Arne Furumark provided archaeologists with a powerful tool for sequencing material from diverse sites.
However, the limitations of Arne Furumark's approach are also rooted in its intellectual origins.
The culture-historical focus on classifying artifacts into discrete cultural packages sometimes led to an oversimplification of complex social processes.

For instance, Arne Furumark's typology, while excellent for formal shape analysis, did not initially address questions of production technology, raw material sourcing, or vessel function, areas that have become central to modern ceramic studies.

The critiques that label Arne Furumark's system as potentially confusing due to its broad categories may stem from an attempt to apply his rigid typological framework to contexts where cultural boundaries were more fluid than his model suggested.
Therefore, Furumark's legacy is inseparable from the intellectual climate of his time.

Arne Furumark was a master of the tools available to him, producing a work of immense utility that nonetheless reflects the theoretical assumptions and limitations of the culture-historical era from which it emerged.
While Arne Furumark is best known for his typological work, his contributions to Aegean prehistory extend significantly beyond the analysis of pottery.

Arne Furumark was an active and engaged field archaeologist whose excavations and regional studies provided crucial data for understanding the broader historical landscape of the Bronze Age Aegean and its periphery.

Arne Furumark's most substantial and influential fieldwork was conducted as part of the Swedish Cyprus Expedition, where he played a key role in defining the character of the Late Bronze Age on the island.
Between 1947 and 1948, and again from 1962 to 1963, Furumark directed excavations at the site of Sinda, located in western Cyprus.
Arne Furumark's work at Sinda was instrumental in reinforcing the "Mycenaean colonisation" paradigm for post-palatial Cyprus.

In his 1944 article, "The Mycenaean IIIC Pottery and its Relation to Cypriote Fabrics," Arne Furumark provided a foundational analysis that directly linked Mycenaean ceramic typology to the local Cypriot fabric, thereby establishing a clear and quantifiable link between the Aegean mainland and the island's material culture during this period.
This work was so central to the expedition's interpretation that it was cited alongside publications by other leading members of the team, such as Erik Gjerstad and Paul Åström.

Further insights from Arne Furumark's Cypriot campaigns were presented in his 1965 paper, "The Excavations at Sinda. Some Historical Results," which connected the ceramic evidence from Sinda to broader interpretations of population movements and socio-political change in post-palatial Cyprus.
In addition to his extensive work in Cyprus, Furumark participated in excavations elsewhere in the eastern Mediterranean.
In 1948, Arne Furumark conducted a short but significant excavation at Hala Sultan Tekke, another important Late Bronze Age site in Cyprus.
During this brief campaign, Arne Furumark discovered a large pithos, adding to the corpus of knowledge about the site's occupation and material culture.
This activity demonstrates Arne Furumark's continued involvement in Cypriot archaeology throughout the 1940s.
Beyond the Aegean, Furumark also pursued research in other regions, showcasing the breadth of his interests.
In 1947, Arne Furumark published *Det äldsta Italien* (The Earliest Italy), a pioneering post-World War II study of Italian prehistory.
This work extended Arne Furumark's methodological expertise beyond the Aegean and contributed to the wider study of the Mediterranean world.
Arne Furumark's scholarly output also included detailed studies of Aegean history itself.

Arne Furumark's 1950 paper, "The Settlement at Ialysos and Aegean History c. 1550–1400 B.C.," was a landmark study that anchored the Late Helladic and Late Minoan ceramic sequences to a specific period.

By doing so, Arne Furumark provided a crucial synchronistic framework that has been invaluable for debates concerning the absolute dating of events like the eruption of Thera, helping to align Aegean chronology with the well-established timelines of the Egyptian Second Intermediate Period and New Kingdom.

Through these varied field projects and regional studies, Furumark demonstrated himself to be a versatile scholar who applied his meticulous methods to a wide range of archaeological contexts, enriching our understanding of the Bronze Age Mediterranean far beyond the confines of his famous pottery typology.

One of the most fascinating aspects of Arne Furumark's career is his active and enthusiastic engagement with the monumental decipherment of Linear B, the script used to write an early form of Greek at sites like Knossos and Pylos.
Far from being a passive observer of this revolution in Aegean studies, Furumark was an integral part of the scholarly network that embraced and disseminated the new knowledge.
Arne Furumark's recognition as an expert in Mycenaean archaeology is evidenced by his inclusion on the targeted distribution list for Michael Ventris's seminal 'Work Note 15' in 1951.

This document, which outlined the phonetic grid methodology and morphological analysis that would lead to the decipherment, was sent to a select group of 31 leading scholars, including prominent figures like Carl Blegen, Alice Kober, and John Chadwick.

Being among this elite cohort immediately after the decipherment was announced publicly by Ventris in a BBC interview on July 1, 1952, signifies that Furumark was considered a key authority whose opinion would carry significant weight within the academic community.
Following the public announcement of the decipherment, Furumark quickly moved to incorporate its findings into his own archaeological interpretations.

Arne Furumark's correspondence with both Michael Ventris and John Chadwick, the latter of whom would famously co-author the definitive grammar of Mycenaean Greek, is preserved in archival collections at the Program in Aegean Scripts and Prehistory (PASP) at the University of Cincinnati and the Uppsala University Archives.

This exchange of letters documents Arne Furumark's early endorsement of the Greek interpretation of Linear B, positioning him as an influential validator of the decipherment within the archaeological world.

Arne Furumark's rapid integration of the new linguistic evidence demonstrates intellectual agility and a clear understanding of how the decipherment would fundamentally reshape the field, overturning Sir Arthur Evans's long-held belief that the language was non-Greek.
Furumark's support for the new interpretation helped legitimize it among his peers.
Furthermore, Furumark's participation in the nascent scholarly community formed around the decipherment was direct and significant.
Arne Furumark attended the first-ever international colloquium on Mycenaean texts, held at Gif-sur-Yvette in France in April 1956.

This conference was a historic gathering, bringing together the pioneers of the field for the first time, and it was the only such event attended by Michael Ventris before his untimely death in September of that year.

Furumark’s presence at this exclusive meeting places him within a small, foundational cohort of scholars, alongside institutional leaders and philologists from across Europe, including Émile Benveniste and Georges Dumézil.
This engagement underscores that Arne Furumark's interest in Aegean scripts was not limited to his primary work on pottery.
Arne Furumark was also deeply involved in the study of the undeciphered Linear A script, publishing a two-volume work on the subject in 1956, *Linear A und die altkretische Sprache*.

Arne Furumark's multifaceted engagement with Aegean writing systems—from applying the new Greek decipherment to his own work to studying the older Minoan script—paints a picture of a truly comprehensive scholar who was at the forefront of the most exciting intellectual developments in classical archaeology during his lifetime.
Arne Furumark's scholarly output was extensive and covered a wide range of topics within Aegean prehistory.
Arne Furumark's publications reflect his dual expertise in ceramic typology and broader historical archaeology, as well as his engagement with the study of Aegean scripts.
*The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification* was published in 1941.
*The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification* is part of a three-volume work.
*The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification* is a foundational typology of Mycenaean pottery forms and shapes.
*The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery* was published in 1941.
*The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery* is part of a three-volume work.
*The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery* establishes a relative chronology for Mycenaean pottery based on stylistic sequences.
*Det äldsta Italien* was published in 1947.
*Det äldsta Italien* is a book.
*Det äldsta Italien* is a pioneering post-WWII research on Italian prehistory.
*The Mycenaean III C Pottery and its Relation to Cypriote Fabrics* was published in 1944.
*The Mycenaean III C Pottery and its Relation to Cypriote Fabrics* is an article in *Opuscula Archaeologica*.
*The Mycenaean III C Pottery and its Relation to Cypriote Fabrics* links Mycenaean ceramic typology to Cypriot fabrics, reinforcing the "colonisation" paradigm.
*The Settlement at Ialysos and Aegean History c. 1550–1400 B.C.* was published in 1950.
*The Settlement at Ialysos and Aegean History c. 1550–1400 B.C.* is an article in *Opuscula Archaeologica*.
*The Settlement at Ialysos and Aegean History c. 1550–1400 B.C.* anchors Aegean chronology to the Egyptian New Kingdom.
*Linear A und die altkretische Sprache* was published in 1956.
*Linear A und die altkretische Sprache* is a two-volume work.
*Linear A und die altkretische Sprache* is a study of the undeciphered Minoan syllabic script.
*Swedish Excavations at Sinda, Cyprus: Excavations Conducted by Arne Furumark 1947–1948* was published in 2003.
*Swedish Excavations at Sinda, Cyprus: Excavations Conducted by Arne Furumark 1947–1948* was co-authored with Charles M. Adelman.
*Swedish Excavations at Sinda, Cyprus: Excavations Conducted by Arne Furumark 1947–1948* is the final publication of Arne Furumark's major excavation project in Cyprus.
*Redan de gamla grekerna* was published in 1961.
*Redan de gamla grekerna* is a popular work on ancient Greeks.
*Hellener och barbarer* was published in 1962.
*Hellener och barbarer* is a popular work on Greeks and barbarians.
*Gods of ancient Crete* was published in 1965.
*Gods of ancient Crete* is an article in *Opuscula Atheniensia*.
*Gods of ancient Crete* is an analysis of religious iconography.
*The excavations at Sinda. Some historical results* was published in 1965.
*The excavations at Sinda. Some historical results* is an article in *Opuscula Atheniensia*.
*The excavations at Sinda. Some historical results* is a presentation of historical interpretations from Arne Furumark's Sinda excavations.
*Foreword to John Chadwick’s Mykenes röst* was published in 1960 / 1961.
*Foreword to John Chadwick’s Mykenes röst* is a foreword.
*Foreword to John Chadwick’s Mykenes röst* is an endorsement of the decipherment of Linear B in a Swedish translation.
Edited Reports were published in 1963.
Edited Reports is an edited volume.
Edited Reports contains excavation reports from the Swedish Institute in Rome (campaigns III-VIII).
Furumark's legacy is that of a foundational figure whose work provided the essential chronological scaffolding for Aegean archaeology for much of the 20th century.
Arne Furumark's 1941 pottery classification remains a touchstone for scholars, a testament to the power of meticulous typological analysis in an earlier phase of the discipline.
While modern methodologies have moved beyond the strictures of culture-historical archaeology, Arne Furumark's system's enduring relevance highlights the quality and comprehensiveness of his work.

At the same time, the critiques leveled against Arne Furumark's system serve as a valuable lesson in the evolution of archaeological thought, illustrating the shift towards more holistic approaches that consider vessel function, technology, and social context.
Beyond his typology, Furumark's legacy is also one of intellectual adaptability and wide-ranging scholarship.

Arne Furumark successfully transitioned from a career focused on material culture to embracing the linguistic revolution of the Linear B decipherment, integrating its findings into his archaeological interpretations with remarkable speed and insight.
Arne Furumark's work in Cyprus, Italy, and on Minoan religion demonstrates a versatility that prevented him from becoming a narrow specialist.
In summary, Arne Furumark was a master of his craft, a leader in his field, and a pivotal figure whose influence continues to be felt in the ongoing study of the ancient Aegean.

**Josef Arne Gerdt Furumark** (26 September 1903 – 8 October 1982) was a Swedish[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAccorinti2014p._323,_n._3-2) archaeologist who specialised in the ceramics of [Mycenaean Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece "Mycenaean Greece"). His three-volume work _The Mycenaean Pottery_ established a categorisation and chronology of the ceramics of the [Late Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Bronze_Age "Late Bronze Age") on the Greek mainland. A 1943 review credited him with doing "for [Mycenaean pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_pottery "Mycenaean pottery") what [Payne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humfry_Payne "Humfry Payne") did for Corinthian and [Beazley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Beazley "John Beazley") for Attic wares",[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDaniel1943252-3) and subsequent scholars have considered the work a standard reference, though it received criticism for an over-rigid approach and for prioritising stylistic analysis at the expense of information about objects' archaeological contexts.

Furumark was born in the Norwegian capital of [Kristiania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") (now Oslo).[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-Union-1) After an unhappy childhood, in which he initially seemed set to follow his father into the paper business, he entered [Uppsala University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala_University "Uppsala University") in Sweden in 1925 to study the humanities, and became a pupil of the archaeologist [Axel W. Persson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axel_W._Persson "Axel W. Persson"). He obtained his doctorate, with a thesis on the decoration of Mycenaean ceramics, in 1939, and became an associate professor at Uppsala in the same year. He led excavations at [Sinda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinta,_Cyprus "Sinta, Cyprus") on Cyprus, the first Swedish archaeological work on the island since the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), between 1947 and 1948, and became a professor at Uppsala in 1952. He remained there until his retirement in 1970, and served a year's term as director of the [Swedish Institute at Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Institute_at_Athens "Swedish Institute at Athens"), a research centre for classical archaeology, between 1956 and 1957. He also conducted excavations at [San Giovenale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Giovenale "San Giovenale") in Italy between 1962 and 1963, and published on the Mycenaean settlement of the island of [Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes "Rhodes").

Although an early sceptic of the idea that the [Linear B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B "Linear B") script was used to write Greek, Furumark corresponded with [Michael Ventris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ventris "Michael Ventris"), who deciphered it in 1953, and was one of the first archaeologists to use his conclusion that its language was indeed Greek. Furumark's work on ceramics helped to establish the distinctive nature of mainland Greek ("Helladic") ceramics in relation to Cretan ("[Minoan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_civilization "Minoan civilization")") wares, and highlighted the ways in which both cultural groups influenced each other to varying extents over time. In doing so, he helped to overturn the narrative of [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans") that Minoan Crete had dominated mainland Greece throughout the Late Bronze Age. He also established continuity between Mycenaean pottery and that of the following [Protogeometric period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protogeometric_style "Protogeometric style"), and thereby that narratives which argued for the complete overturning of Greek culture at the end of the Bronze Age, such as that of the [Dorian invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_invasion "Dorian invasion"), were incorrect.

Josef Arne Gerdt Furumark was born on 26 September 1903,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000112-4) in the Norwegian capital of [Kristiania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") (now Oslo),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-5)[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-Union-1) where his father worked as a businessman in the paper industry.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198334-7) He suffered from a skin condition throughout his life, which left him shy and socially isolated.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198338-8) Family life during his early years was unhappy; Furumark initially attended business school in Norway and worked in his father's offices in Oslo and in London, where at the age of nineteen he visited the [British Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum"). He later said that this visit encouraged him to change his studies to archaeology. In 1925, he entered Sweden's [Uppsala University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala_University "Uppsala University"), where he studied a wide [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities "Humanities") curriculum including classical archaeology, philosophy and theology. He eventually came to study there under the Mycenaean archaeologist [Axel W. Persson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axel_W._Persson "Axel W. Persson"),[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198334-7) under whom he took part in excavations in Greece.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9)

Furumark received his doctorate, with a dissertation on the subject of [Mycenaean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece "Mycenaean Greece") ceramic decoration, in 1939. In the same year, he was made an associate professor at Uppsala.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9) In 1941, he published _The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification_ and _The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery,_[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) a two-volume study which analysed, categorised and dated Late Bronze Age ceramics from the mainland of Greece according to their shapes and decorative motifs.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) He had begun writing a third volume, _Mycenaean Pottery: A History,_ by 1941, but abandoned the project by 1944.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas201814-12) He published _Det äldsta Italien_, a handbook of Italian archaeology, in 1947, which became widely cited: he planned, but never published, an edition in English.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197630-13)

Between 1947 and 1948, Furumark excavated at [Sinda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinta,_Cyprus "Sinta, Cyprus") on Cyprus.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) Swedish archaeologists had excavated widely on the island before the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), but Furumark's was the first Swedish project there after 1945.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStyrenius19948%E2%80%9312-14) The excavation was conducted in two campaigns; the first from 22 December 1947 to 22 January 1948, and the second from 25 March to 7 May 1948.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFurumark200363-15) [Carl-Gustaf Styrenius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl-Gustaf_Styrenius "Carl-Gustaf Styrenius") later credited Furumark's excavations with expanding scholarly knowledge of migration from Greece to Cyprus at the end of the Bronze Age.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStyrenius199412-16) The project uncovered a [Late Cypriot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Cypriot "Late Cypriot") (c. 1300 – c. 1200 BCE) settlement with [Cyclopean walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclopean_masonry "Cyclopean masonry"),[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEG%C3%B6ransson2012419-17) though only excavated a small fraction of its total area of around 46,500 square metres (11.5 acres).[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIacovou200710-18) In 1948, during a visit to the Bronze Age site of [Hala Sultan Tekke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hala_Sultan_Tekke_/(archaeological_site/) "Hala Sultan Tekke (archaeological site)") on the island, he noticed a large [pithos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pithos "Pithos") in a field, which prompted new excavations around it.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%85str%C3%B6m1978232-19)

In 1950, Furumark argued, on the basis of the ceramics of Minoan Crete, that the idea of the Cretan site of [Knossos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knossos "Knossos") being ruled by Greek-speakers in the Late Minoan II period (c. 1490 – c. 1430 BCE) was "untenable":[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-20) the fact of mainland rule over Crete in this period was established two years later by [the discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decipherment_of_Linear_B "Decipherment of Linear B") by [Michael Ventris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ventris "Michael Ventris") that the [Linear B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B "Linear B") tablets made there at this time were written in a form of Greek.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990314-21) Furumark had maintained a correspondence with Ventris since 1951;[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHedlund200310-22) after Ventris proposed his decipherment, Furumark worked with [Gudmund Björck](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gudmund_Bj%C3%B6rck&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gudmund Björck (page does not exist)") ([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudmund_Bj%C3%B6rck "sv:Gudmund Björck")), the professor of Greek at Uppsala, to check its accuracy. The two wrote to Ventris in October 1952 to give their verdict that he was correct.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHedlund200311-23)[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-25) Furumark was one of the first archaeologists to use his decipherment in his own work.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-ArtHistDict-26)[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-28) Also in 1950, he argued that Mycenaean settlers had arrived on the island of [Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes "Rhodes") around the turn of the Late Helladic IIB and IIIA periods (that is, c. 1400 BCE), that they lived peacefully alongside the pre-existing population, who used [Minoan pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_pottery "Minoan pottery"), and were allowed to live in existing houses. Mario Benzi, in 1988, called this idea "astonishing", and suggested that the Mycenaean incomers more probably subjugated the inhabitants by force.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBenzi198859-29)

Furumark became Professor of Classical Archaeology and Ancient History at [Uppsala University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala_University "Uppsala University") in 1952,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476Medwid2000112-30) succeeding Persson.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%85str%C3%B6m20037-31) In the early years of his professorship, he was involved in reorganising the university's collection of antiquities,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9) and created a small museum in two of the university's rooms.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197631-32) He served as director of the [Swedish Institute at Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Institute_at_Athens "Swedish Institute at Athens"), a research centre for classical archaeology, between 1956 and 1957.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAccorinti2014p._323,_n._3-2) Among his students at Uppsala were [Margareta Lindgren](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margareta_Lindgren&action=edit&redlink=1 "Margareta Lindgren (page does not exist)"), who worked on Linear B,[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoschEnegren2017xxviii-33) and [Gisela Walberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gisela_Walberg&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gisela Walberg (page does not exist)"), who extended his work on Mycenaean ceramics to those of [Middle Minoan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Minoan "Middle Minoan") Crete,[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHood1978375-34) as well as [Sture Brunnsåker](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sture_Brunns%C3%A5ker&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sture Brunnsåker (page does not exist)") ([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sture_Brunns%C3%A5ker "sv:Sture Brunnsåker")) and [Carl Nylander](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Nylander&action=edit&redlink=1 "Carl Nylander (page does not exist)") ([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Nylander "sv:Carl Nylander")).[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197631-32) His own academic work during his professorship, in contrast to his previous studies of Mycenaean and Italian archaeology, focused on the ancient Aegean scripts.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197630%E2%80%9331-35) In 1956, he gave a lecture in Berlin in which he attempted to decipher the [Linear A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_A "Linear A") tablets uncovered at the site of [Hagia Triada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Triada "Hagia Triada") on Crete,[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacKendrick1981120-36) using the methods applied by Ventris to Linear B,[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBraidwoodMason195859-37) and posited that Linear A had similarities with the Anatolian [Indo-European language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-European_languages "Indo-European languages") of [Luwian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luwian_language "Luwian language").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacKendrick1981120-36)[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-39) He was appointed a member of the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") in 1958.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPohl1958412-40) Between 1962 and 1963, he excavated at [San Giovenale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Giovenale "San Giovenale") in Italy,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) continuing excavations begun there in the 1950s by the [Swedish Institute in Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Institute_in_Rome "Swedish Institute in Rome").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKarlsson200622-41) After recovering from a period of serious illness in the late 1960s,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9) he retired from his professorship in 1970,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476Medwid2000112-30) and was succeeded by his former student Sture Brunnsåker.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197631-32) He died on 8 October 1982 in Uppsala.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000112-4)

Contributions to archaeology
----------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arne_Furumark&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Contributions to archaeology")\]

[![Image 4: Goblet-shaped ceramic vessel, with a tall stem and two handles, painted in black with a squid design](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Cup_squid_1300-1200_BC_Staatliche_Antikensammlungen.jpg/250px-Cup_squid_1300-1200_BC_Staatliche_Antikensammlungen.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cup_squid_1300-1200_BC_Staatliche_Antikensammlungen.jpg)

Mycenaean [kylix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kylix "Kylix") of the Late Helladic IIIB period

Johannes Siapkas, in 2022, identified Furumark as part of a Swedish tradition, traceable back to the work of [Erik Hedén](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Erik_Hed%C3%A9n&action=edit&redlink=1 "Erik Hedén (page does not exist)") ([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_Hed%C3%A9n "sv:Erik Hedén")) at the turn of the twentieth century, to distinguish the academic treatment of the ancient world from the popular understanding of it, and to prioritise scientific objectivity in its reconstruction.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas2022114-42) A 1943 review of _The Mycenaean Pottery_ credited him with doing "for Mycenaean pottery what [Payne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humfry_Payne "Humfry Payne") did for Corinthian and [Beazley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Beazley "John Beazley") for Attic wares";[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDaniel1943252-3) Siapkas compared his work with that of [Johann Joachim Winckelmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Joachim_Winckelmann "Johann Joachim Winckelmann") on ancient sculpture.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas20187-43)

_The Mycenaean Pottery_ was the first complete survey of its subject published in book form,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) and became the established point of departure for subsequent studies.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas20187-43) Furumark's approach developed from that of German stylistic analysis, known as _Strukturforschung_ ('Structural Research'), first practised in the 1920s by archaeologists such as [Friedrich Matz](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Friedrich_Matz_\(born_1890\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Friedrich Matz (born 1890) (page does not exist)") ([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Matz_der_J%C3%BCngere "de:Friedrich Matz der Jüngere")).[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-45) However, Furumark rejected the association made in _Strukturforschung_, under the influence of [Nazi racial theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_racial_theories "Nazi racial theories"), between cultural styles and biological races.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas201815-46) As well as ceramic vessels, he named and categorised the terracotta figurines known as [psi, phi, and tau types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psi,_phi_and_tau_type_figurine "Psi, phi and tau type figurine").[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench1971103-47) The archaeologist [Robin Hägg](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robin_H%C3%A4gg&action=edit&redlink=1 "Robin Hägg (page does not exist)") ([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_H%C3%A4gg_/(arkeolog/) "sv:Robin Hägg (arkeolog)")) described the books as Furumark's "_magnum opus_ ... \[and\] ever since the standard work on this topic";[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) Linda Medwid called them "the definitive reference on the subject" in 2000.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48) Although the [absolute dates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_dating "Absolute dating") of Furumark's chronology have generally been revised, the categories and reference he assigned to particular shapes and motifs remain conventional vocabulary within the field.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2011258-49)

Furumark's contemporary [Alan Wace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Wace "Alan Wace") criticised him for what he called "excessive [pigeonholing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeonholing "Pigeonholing")" of ceramic styles, and for ignoring information about the archaeological contexts in which finds were unearthed; the latter criticism was also articulated by Wace's collaborator [Carl Blegen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Blegen "Carl Blegen").[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas20187-43) [Susan Sherratt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Sherratt "Susan Sherratt"), in 2021, criticised Furumark's approach as "essentially stylistically based and unrealistically over-analytical", particularly by contrast with that of [Lisa French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_French "Elizabeth French"), who worked on Mycenaean pottery in the second half of the twentieth century.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2021-50) [Gerald Cadogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gerald_Cadogan_\(archaeologist\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gerald Cadogan (archaeologist) (page does not exist)") described Furumark's approach as _[dirigiste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirigiste "Dirigiste")_ for what he considered its excessive devotion to ordered categorisation.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTECadogan2003353-51)[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-53) Sherratt elsewhere criticised Furumark's system for lumping together variations of shape and motif into single categories, on the basis of what he considered to be evolutionary relationships between them.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2011258-49) She also disagreed with his treatment of individual motifs and shapes in isolation, rather than as part of coherent decorative schemes.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2011259-54)

### Influence on Minoan and Mycenaean studies

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arne_Furumark&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Influence on Minoan and Mycenaean studies")\]

[![Image 5: Tall, wide-necked vessel decorated with a simple geometric drawing of a chariot.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Amphoroid_krater_with_chariot_scene%2C_1300-1250_BC%2C_AM_of_Nafplio%2C_202188.jpg/250px-Amphoroid_krater_with_chariot_scene%2C_1300-1250_BC%2C_AM_of_Nafplio%2C_202188.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Amphoroid_krater_with_chariot_scene,_1300-1250_BC,_AM_of_Nafplio,_202188.jpg)

Mycenaean [krater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krater "Krater") from the Late Helladic IIIC period, as defined by Furumark

[![Image 6: Vessel decorated with simple geometric drawings of horses.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Horses_manger_Louvre_A513.jpg/250px-Horses_manger_Louvre_A513.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Horses_manger_Louvre_A513.jpg)

Furumark argued that the ceramics of the [Mycenaean civilisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_civilisation "Mycenaean civilisation") of mainland Greece were a development of pre-Mycenaean mainland forms, with influence from contemporary Minoan Crete.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000112-4) This aligned with the view set forth by Wace and Blegen in 1918, that the civilisation of mainland Greece had been broadly continuous and indigenous throughout the Bronze Age. This view, known as the "Helladic Heresy" ("Helladic" meaning "native to mainland Greece"),[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaceBlegen1918118%E2%80%93119Galanakis2007241-55) was itself an extension of the archaeological theory of [Christos Tsountas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christos_Tsountas "Christos Tsountas"), who argued for the continuity of Greek culture from prehistory to the modern period.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPliatsika2020292-56) Furumark established the sub-periods of the [Helladic chronology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helladic_chronology "Helladic chronology") based on the stages of development of pottery styles, which became the standard [relative chronology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_dating "Relative dating") system used in studies of the Mycenaean period.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11)

Furumark's findings contradicted the idea of [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans"), who had named Minoan civilisation in the early 20th century, that Mycenaean civilisation had developed from that of Crete.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113Galanakis2007240-57) Furumark concluded that the level of Minoan influence in mainland ceramics changed over time, with an overall balance roughly even between Cretan- and indigenous-derived vessel shapes, a high level of Cretan influence in the Late Helladic IIIA period (c. 1400 – c. 1300 BCE), and a dominant mainland influence in the following Late Helladic IIIIB period (c. 1300 – c. 1180 BCE).[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-58) He therefore rejected both the term "Late Minoan", used for mainland pottery of the Late Bronze Age by Evans and [Duncan Mackenzie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Mackenzie "Duncan Mackenzie"),[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) and Wace and Blegen's "Helladic", which he considered to imply that developments on the mainland were isolated from the wider Aegean. Since Furumark's work, the terms "Helladic" and "Mycenaean" have been considered equivalent,[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48) though his belief that "Helladic" did not adequately encompass the influence of Crete and the other Aegean islands has generally been rejected by other scholars.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11)

Medwid called _The Mycenaean Pottery_ "a final refutation" of Evans's view that Mycenaean Greece had been subordinate to Minoan Crete, referencing Furumark's demonstration of the continuity of Mycenaean pottery as well as that certain Mycenaean forms, such as the [kylix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kylix "Kylix"), were adopted on Crete.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48) Following the 1938 work of Mogens B. Mackeprang,[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-59) Furumark included two styles of pottery, found by Wace at Mycenae and labelled by him the Granary Style and the Close Style, in his categorisation of the Late Helladic IIIC period (c. 1180 – c. 1050 BCE).[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-60) He identified a trend in the later part of the period towards simple geometric designs,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) establishing continuity between Mycenaean pottery and that of the following [Protogeometric period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protogeometric_style "Protogeometric style"), and thereby that narratives which argued for complete cultural collapse or replacement at the end of the Bronze Age, such as that of the [Dorian invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_invasion "Dorian invasion"), were incorrect.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48)

4.title: Furumark, Arne - Dictionary of Art Historians
4.description: Archaeologist, specialist in late Aegean Bronze Age art; professor at Uppsala University 1952-70. Furumark's major work, The Chronology of Mycenaean Potter
4.content:
![Image 1: Man is sitting on the excavation of archaeological remains with a pickaxe in one hand and a brush in the other](https://arthistorians.info/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Arne-Furumark-1948.jpg)

**Image Credit:**[Upsala Universitet](https://www.uu.se/en/gustavianum/our-collections/the-historical-collections/classical-archaeology/swedish-excavations-at-sinda)

**Full Name:** Furumark, Arne

**Gender:** male

**Date Born:** 1903

**Date Died:** 1982

**Home Country/ies:** Sweden

**Subject Area(s):** Aegean, ancient, archaeology, bronzes (visual works), and metalwork (visual works)

### Overview

Archaeologist, specialist in late Aegean Bronze Age art; professor at Uppsala University 1952-70. Furumark’s major work, _The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery_ appeared in 1941. It remains the standard work on the subject. After World War II, his innovative research into the prehistory of Italy was published in 1947 as _Detäldsa Italien_. He excavated Cyprus 1947-48 (at Sinda). In 1950 his “Settlement at Ialysos and Aegean History c. 1550-1400 BC,” was published. He was director of the Swedish Institute in Athens, 1956-57. Furumark returned to Cypriot excavations 1962-63.Furumark employed Ventri’s desciphering of Linear B for his own work; he was one of the first. _Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery_ made use of formal shape typologies to date the pottery. “Furumark” 1 through 333 is used internationally in the description of Mycenean and Minoan pottery.

### Selected Bibliography

[complete writings:] Hägg, Robin. “The published writings of Arne Furumark: A bibliography.” in Arne Furumark dedicata. _Acta Instituti Atheniensis Regni Sueciae Series in quarto_. _Opuscula Atheniensia_ VIII (1968): 213-17; _The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery_. Stockholm: Kungl. Vitterhets, historie och antikvitets akademien,1941; _The Mycenaean Pottery, Analysis and Classification_. Stockholm: Kungl. Vitterhets, historie och antikvitets akademien, 1941;[those two previous volumes appearing again, with new plates, as] _Mycenaean Pottery_. Skrifter utgivna av Svenska institutet i Athen. Stockholm: s.n, 1972-1992.

### Sources

Hägg, Robin. “Furumark, Arne.” _Encyclopedia of the History of Classical Archaeology_. Nancy Thomson de Grummond, ed. Westport, CT: Greenwood Press, 1996, vol. 1, p. 476; Furumark, Arne, and Adelman, Charles M. _Swedish Excavations at Sinda, Cyprus: Excavations Conducted by Arne Furumark 1947-1948_. Stockholm: Paul Åströms Förlag, 2003.

8.content:
The Program in Aegean Scripts and Prehistory (PASP) was founded in 1986 by Thomas G. Palaima as a research center pertaining to the use of writing in Minoan Crete (Cretan Hieroglyphic and Linear A ca. 1850-1450 BCE), Mycenaean Greece and Mycenaeanized Crete (Linear B ca. 1450-1200 BCE) and the island of Cyprus (Cypro-Minoan in the Bronze Age and Cypriote Syllabic script in the historical period ca. 1500-1200 BCE and 750-225 BCE respectively). The setting up of PASP was supported by the Comité International pour les Études Myceniennes, the governing international body for work on these writing systems, their texts and their cultures.

A strength of PASP is that it is part of a graduate research program in the Department of Classics at University of Texas at Austin, a major research university. PASP does not grant its own degrees, but provides graduate students in the UT program who are receiving broad training in all areas of Classical civilization with the opportunity to do specialized research at a high level in areas of Aegean and eastern Mediterranean prehistory and archaeology pertaining to inscribed or marked materials. It also facilitates work by visiting scholars, junior and senior, American and foreign.

PASP has also now helped set up at the University of Texas at Austin a consortium of scholars (professors and graduate students) interested in historical inscriptions and early scripts (Mesopotamian, Anatolian, Syro-Palestinian, Egyptian, Latin, Greek, Mayan, Arabic) in order to present and critique papers in progress. This ‘Scripts Institute’ is called the Institute for the Study of Writing Systems and Decipherment.

PASP resources:

(1) A full, but not complete, archives of 1:1 scale photographs of Linear B and Linear A (and Cretan Hieroglyphic) inscriptions (and some Cypro-Minoan and Cypriote Syllabic). The collection also includes color images of selected Knossos and Pylos tablets and of the Khania stirrup jars.

(2) offprint collections from distinguished Mycenaean scholars at the University of Wisconsin (E.L. Bennett, Jr.) and Cambridge University (Frank Stubbings), as well as other sources (e.g., T.B.L. Webster). These have been catalogued and cross-referenced via computer. They contain materials going back to the turn of the century and are a wonderful research tool. The collection has been kept fairly current 1985-present via contributions of offprints to PASP by scholars worldwide, especially connected with the analytical bibliographical journal _Studies in Mycenaean Inscriptions and Dialect_, which PASP revived in the early 1990’s.

(3) microfilms of important excavations (Pylos, Knossos) and of the original work notes of Michael Ventris, the scholar credited with the decipherment of Linear B in June 1952.

(4) the letters from Michael Ventris to Emmett L. Bennett, Jr.; letters to Alice E. Kober (a senior contemporary of Ventris and arguably the leading scholar in this field until her death on September 16, 1950) from Sir John Myres, Michael Ventris, Emmett L. Bennett, Jr., and John Franklin Daniel, among others (xeroxes of correspondence with Johannes Sundwall); the papers and indices of Alice Kober; the early papers and tablet photographs of E.L. Bennett, Jr.; annotated books from the library of Leonard Palmer; and the scholarly papers pertinent to Aegean scripts of William Brice and Elizabeth Barber).

All these scholars were in the forefront of work on and subsequent to the decipherment of Linear B. We also have xeroxed copies of the correspondence of Arne Furumark, and other primary or photocopied original research papers. Among special treasures that have been exhibited periodically are the letter of Michael Ventris of June 18, 1952 announcing to Emmett L. Bennett, Jr., his decipherment of Linear B and showing how it worked; the 186,000 hand-cut note cards of Alice E. Kober and a copy of her dissertation; the ms. Version of unpublished _Scripta Minoa III_ (we now have a letter from Ventris to William Brice about this); a copy of the famous Ventris Mid-Century report; a copy of the autopsy report on the death of Michael Ventris on September 7, 1956.

PASP wishes to acknowledge in particular the great help of Sue Trombley, Christy Costlow Moilanen, Zachary Smith, Sarah Buchanan, Garrett Bruner, Nicole Inskeep, and Dygo Tosa in systematizing and preserving and imaging PASP’s archival material.

(5) some casts of Linear B and Cypro-Minoan texts.

(6) primary reference works on Aegean prehistoric inscriptions, the history of writing, early Greek language and Cypriote archaeology.

All published Mycenological colloquia, specialized journals, corpus volumes and editions of tablets (including those in progress) are ready to hand, along with many specialized monographs in linguistics and on aspects of Minoan and Mycenaean cultures. These supplement holdings in the Classics archaeological seminar, reference room and library, which are all located on the same floor of Waggener Hall as PASP and house all but the most specialized archaeological journals and monographs. The university graduate library, located a five-minute walk away, is one of the largest in the USA. Some peculiar gaps have been rectified, e.g., by the acquisition of a complete run of RDAC (Cypriote holdings being weakest, but still considerable). The reference collection has been made full by the addition of books from the collections of Leonard R. Palmer and Emmett L. Bennett, Jr., and by judicious acquisitions over the twenty-eight years of PASP’s existence.

Abstract

![Image 8: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)AI




--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This chapter reviews Greek pottery from the Late Bronze Age (LBA) and Early Iron Age (EIA), focusing on chronological and typological features, ceramic production, circulation, and consumption. Organized into three phases, it highlights significant contributions from Arne Furumark while emphasizing overlooked aspects such as raw materials and forming techniques, which are crucial for understanding pottery styles beyond mere decoration.

Key takeaways

![Image 9: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)AI




-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  This chapter reviews Greek pottery from the Late Bronze Age and Early Iron Age, covering 14th to 8th centuries.
2.  It organizes the discussion into three phases: Mycenaean Palatial, Postpalatial, and Early Iron Age.
3.  Furumark's contributions to Mycenaean pottery research emphasize style, but overlook raw materials and techniques.
4.  Understanding pottery style involves examining less visible attributes, such as forming techniques and technologies.
5.  The focus is on central and southern Aegean ceramic developments, excluding northern and southeastern regions.

After several decades of archaeometric investigations on Early Bronze Age pottery, now is the time to bring these manifold results and experts together for a holistic approach of a broader region through socio-cultural interpretations. The archaeometric approach to pottery in the (Greek) Aegean is based on a long tradition and nowadays forms a well-established scientific field in Bronze Age archaeology in that region. Thanks to various research groups and their longterm engagement in developing the methodological and theoretical background – such as the Fitch Laboratory of the British School and the Demokritos lab in Athens, the University of Bonn, and Sheffield University – pottery experts in the Aegean are now able to use various scientific methods based on a well-established scientific framework and comparable data. This state-ofthe-art interdisciplinary approach for Aegean ceramics not only produces a large amount of new and complex data, which are mainly used by specialists in this field, but also leads to a multifaceted picture hardly manageable by non-experts for their socio-cultural follow-up interpretations. Our main aim is focused on combining the archaeometric experts and their scientific questions and data to gain a broader archaeological-cultural contextualisation within one particular time horizon.

The present paper deals with the wheel-based manufacturing technology employed for the production of pottery in central Laconia and the Argolid during the Mycenaean palatial period (roughly 1450-1200 BCE). The main set of data comes from the combined macroscopic and X-Ray analyses on pottery discovered at the palace of Ayios Vasileios in Laconia. Additional material of Argive/NE Peloponnesian provenance was examined as well for comparative reasons. The latter comes from Tiryns and Tall Zirā'a, Jordan. Although growing evidence suggests that wheel-forming techniques can be more variable than one would have traditionally thought, very few studies have examined the use of the potter's wheel during the Mycenaean period and the underlying craft behaviours. Our study suggests that the knowledge of this tool in the Argolid and central Laconia was not associated with the wheel-throwing technique but the so-called wheel-coiling, and was based on similar levels of expertise. However, we can also observe variations between these two regions, especially in the ways of mastering the rotary device within the forming process. The manufacture of the wheelmade pottery in Mycenaean Greece implies thus a complex technological phenomenon that involved different potting communities participating in the social and economic organization of palatial pottery production.

What are the main phases of Greek pottery from the LBA to EIA?add

The study identifies three main phases: Mycenaean Palatial (14th-13th centuries), Postpalatial (12th-mid-11th centuries), and Early Iron Age (mid-11th-8th centuries). Each phase displays unique chronological and typological features.

How did Arne Furumark influence the understanding of Mycenaean pottery?add

Furumark's seminal work from 1941 defined Mycenaean pottery broadly and set a foundation for chronological and stylistic analysis. However, it did not fully address raw materials and production techniques, which remain underexplored.

What gaps exist in the research on Mycenaean pottery production?add

The paper highlights a lack of focus on raw materials and forming techniques crucial for understanding pottery styles. These aspects can provide insights into individual workshops and broader technological developments.

How has ceramic production evolved from the Mycenaean to the Early Iron Age?add

The chapter suggests that ceramic production became increasingly differentiated, reflecting changing social and economic structures from the Mycenaean to Early Iron Age periods. This evolution suggests a shift in consumption patterns and regional practices.

Why are grave goods significant for understanding Mycenaean pottery?add

Grave goods allow for the identification of pottery assemblages, crucial for contextualizing stylistic and chronological developments. This methodology, emphasized by Furumark, has been foundational in the study of Mycenaean pottery.

The island of Samos occupies a key position between the central Aegean and western Anatolia during the third millennium BC. A recent study of the substantial pottery assemblages from the pivotal site of Heraion has defined a rich stratigraphy covering the entire Early Bronze Age (EBA). Currently the only known EBA site on Samos, Heraion has provided the opportunity to undertake a holistic ceramic study with the aim of defining and characterizing local pottery production and, by extension, determining for the first time a secure provenance of suspected imported vessels, through the application of an integrated typological/morphological, macroscopic and microscopic (ceramic petrography) analytical methodology. This diachronic ceramic study, alongside a comparative fabric study of pottery of known origin from a number of contemporary sites, shows clear evidence for the exchange/importation of specific vessel shapes and, in the case of the collared jars, presumably their contents. This enables the reconstruction of patterns of interaction during the later phases of EB II, when there was a particular acceleration in the movement of goods. The present paper draws on a distinctive ceramic class (blue and red schist/phyllite fabrics/wares) and vessel types (transport jars with incised/slashed handles and beaked jugs with a two‐stage neck profile) particular to the EB II late period and discusses them in relation to already published or analysed data from selected Cycladic and Anatolian sites.
